title: Properties, naming conventions, and inspecting object state
sources: Python 3.14 Tutorial, Classes: private variables and name mangling; Python 3.14 built-in functions: property(), vars(), getattr(); Python 3.14 Data Model: custom instances; reviewed 2026-10-03
masterChecklist: Encapsulation conventions, properties, name mangling, __dict__, introspection
whyItMatters: A progress percentage must not become 300 through an ordinary assignment. A property can keep that rule in one place, while introspection helps diagnose state without mistaking naming conventions for a security boundary.
simpleExplanation: A single leading underscore, such as _percent, asks callers to treat a name as an internal detail; Python does not block access. A double leading underscore, such as __token, is rewritten inside the class to a name like _ClassName__token to reduce accidental collisions in subclasses. It is not encryption or access control. A property lets code read or assign obj.percent while Python runs a getter or setter. A setter should validate before changing stored state. For an ordinary instance with a dictionary, vars(obj) and obj.__dict__ show its own stored attributes. getattr(obj, name) can read an attribute by string but may run a property or other descriptor; inspect only trusted objects/names, never dump private values into logs. Some classes use slots and have no instance __dict__.
mentalModel: The object is a small machine. A property is a guarded control dial; the underscore is a 'service personnel' label, not a lock. The instance dictionary is a diagnostic panel, not a public data contract.
outcomes: Validate a value through a property setter.
Explain why a single or double leading underscore is not security.
Inspect ordinary instance attributes without logging secrets.
Recognize that not every object has __dict__ and that getattr may execute code.

realWorldExample.scenario: A learning dashboard stores completion percentage and an internal audit marker.
realWorldExample.riskWithoutSetup: A careless assignment can store an impossible percentage, and a generic vars(obj) logger can expose internal metadata.
realWorldExample.professionalApproach: Use a property for the range invariant, keep diagnostics narrow and allowlisted, and avoid treating name mangling as secrecy.

explanation: The constructor uses the same setter as later assignments, so both paths enforce the range.
type(value) is int intentionally rejects booleans; isinstance(True, int) would be True in Python.
The diagnostic prints only allowlisted state names and never the internal marker's value. Double-underscore rewriting avoids a subclass-name collision but does not make the value secret.
After invalid True is rejected, the previous valid percentage remains 50.
workedExample.safeExperiment: Try setting -1 and 100. Confirm the invalid attempt leaves the prior state unchanged; do not print the internal marker.

procedure: Write down the invariant, such as whole-number percentages from 0 through 100.
Store the backing value under a conventional internal name and expose a property.
Validate before writing so rejected assignments preserve the previous state.
Use vars(obj) or obj.__dict__ only for ordinary instances that have a dictionary, and select safe fields before display.
Use double-underscore names only to avoid accidental subclass collisions, never as a secrets vault.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using isinstance(value, int) when a boolean must be rejected.
commonMistakes.why: bool subclasses int, so True passes that check.
commonMistakes.avoid: Use type(value) is int for this intentionally narrow input contract, or state explicitly that booleans are accepted.

commonMistakes.why: Name mangling only rewrites the attribute name and can be inspected.
commonMistakes.avoid: Keep real secrets outside diagnostic object dumps; use access controls at the system boundary.

commonMistakes.mistake: Logging vars(obj) or calling getattr on arbitrary names from untrusted input.
commonMistakes.why: It can disclose internal state, and attribute access may execute property or descriptor code.
commonMistakes.avoid: Allowlist safe diagnostic fields and use only trusted names and objects.

lab.title: Guard a progress value and inspect only safe state
lab.safety: Fictional in-memory progress only; never log actual account metadata or secrets.
lab.starterCode:
class Progress:
    def __init__(self, percent=0):
        self.__audit_marker = 'internal-demo'
        self.percent = percent

    # Add a percent property and validated setter.

item = Progress(25)
# Set to 50, inspect only safe state names, reject True, then print percent.
guidedSteps: Add @percent.setter and reject values whose exact type is not int or whose range is outside 0..100.
Set item.percent to 50 and print it.
Print only the safe _percent attribute name from vars(item); do not print the audit marker.
Attempt item.percent = True and confirm ValueError; print the unchanged percentage.
checks: The internal marker value is never printed.
A 0 or 100 assignment succeeds; -1, 101 and True fail.
hints: Use type(value) is not int or not 0 <= value <= 100.
Filter names from vars(item) rather than printing the whole mapping.
lab.solutionExplanation: The property enforces the invariant on both construction and assignment. The diagnostic allowlists the safe backing-field name, and the rejected boolean does not change state.
challenges: Predict whether isinstance(True, int) is True and why that matters here.
Find the bug in a setter that assigns _percent before checking its range.
Experiment with a class defining __slots__ and observe whether vars(instance) works.

projectConnection.milestone: Use a validated progress property and narrow diagnostic fields without exposing internal audit data.
projectConnection.definitionOfDone: Normal assignments preserve 0..100 integer state, rejected values do not mutate it, and a test confirms diagnostic output omits internal marker values.

assessment.question: Does a double-underscore attribute make a secret inaccessible?
assessment.answer: No. It is name mangling for collision avoidance, not a security boundary.
assessment.explanation: The rewritten name can be inspected and read.

assessment.question: Why reject True explicitly from an integer percentage?
assessment.answer: Because bool is a subclass of int in Python, so isinstance(True, int) succeeds.
assessment.explanation: The intended contract is an actual whole-number percentage, not a boolean flag.

assessment.question: Should a diagnostic log print vars(obj) for a user record?
assessment.explanation: The instance dictionary may include sensitive or internal attributes.
